newsitem.title: USA: Negative job review requires the right approach.
newsitem.headline: Negative job review requires the right approach.

text.p: Savvy managers can prevent employees from becoming angry or explosive over a negative job review -- if they present it the right way.

"Managers don't like to give negative employment reviews," said Deanna Geddes, a human resources professor at Temple University in Philadelphia. But many companies were asking more of employees than ever before and also issuing more negative evaluations than in the past, she noted.

"The employee's response is, 'You mess with me, I'll mess with you,'" she said. "There's a fair amount of sabotage that goes on in the work place. Sometimes it's a retaliatory response to negative feedback."

Negative appraisals often touch on employee notions of fairness, she said, noting employees may think something like, "Here I am working my tail off and you're saying I'm not good enough when I've never worked harder in my life."
"In the delivery of any bad news, we have to be very sensitive, respectful and careful," she said.

Poor performance review procedures were among the factors said to trigger work place violence, according to 3,000 managers polled by the International Facility Management Association, a Houston-based group that helps companies manage people and other assets.
psychologist Hendrie Weisinger, associated with Excellence In Training Corp., Des Moines, Iowa, cited "unfair" evaluations as among the "leading causes of work place anger."

"There are many examples of employees who become violent when the performance review resembles a parent-child relationship" rather than "a collaborative conversation," said Charles Labig, author of "Preventing Violence in the Workplace" (Amacom), and a consultant in Los Angeles.
"Companies need to look at how managers set the tone in which performance reviews occur," Labig said.

Geddes said managers increasingly were using negative appraisals to eliminate people from the work place. "It used to be that if you performed well, you kept your job. That's not necessarily true" any longer.
Fearful of downsizing, employees recognise the implications of a negative evaluation and may become extremely upset, authorities said.

"It's OK for managers to set high performance standards for employees and to terminate people who don't do their jobs properly or follow company standards," said Rickey Griffin, director of Texas A&M's Centre for Human Resource Management.
"But managers have to acknowledge that the way they do those things may be a contributing factor to work place violence," he said.
Performance evaluations became vogue 40 years ago "and really took off the in the early 1970s," said Dan Holland, an industrial psychologist with Towers Perrin, a human resources consulting firm.
He said most companies do them on systems ranging from the "napkin over lunch" variety to computer-based formats, and that they "vary tremendously in terms of frankness."

"If a manager has done a good job in providing feedback all along the way, there should be no surprises," Holland said. "But managers are busy and some don't feel comfortable doing it. You increase your likelihood of angry action if you take employees by surprise."
"People don't like surprises at work," said Ken Palladino, a veteran supervisor in the Torrington, Conn., post office.

"If it gets to the point where there's a bad performance evaluation, you're a bad manager," he said. "Long before that time, you should have been telling him along the way what his deficiencies were."
"The bottom line," said Temple University's Geddes, "is to try to have companies re-evaluate their appraisal practices."
If managers are sensitive to employees' egos and working conditions that should make an employee more receptive to feedback and more likely to perceive it as fair and accurate.
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
